\[\{{\mathrm{gr}}_r\,T_{i,j}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant m+n, r>s_{i,j}\}.\]

Since ${\mathrm{gr}}\,{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$ is free supercommutative on generators \eqref{eq:gr-img-d}--\eqref{eq:gr-img-f}, the elements $\{{\mathrm{gr}}_r\,T_{i,j}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant m+n, r>s_{i,j}\}$ also freely generate ${\mathrm{gr}}\,{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove it using the same argument as in \cite[Prop.~2.7]{LM21}. Let
\[
\mathbf D_i^{(2)}:=D_i^{(2)}-\frac12(D_i^{(1)})^2-\frac12D_i^{(1)},
\]
then by \eqref{dr3}, we have $[\mathbf D_i^{(2)},E_i^{(r)}]=\mathfrak{s}_iE_i^{(r+1)}$. Note that $D_i^{(2)}=\mathsf{T}_{i,i}^{(2)}-\sum_{j<i}\mathsf{T}_{i,j}^{(1)}\mathsf{T}_{j,i}^{(1)}$ and $D_i^{(1)}=\mathsf{T}_{i,i}^{(1)}$. A direct computation implies that
\begin{align*}
\Delta(\mathbf D_i^{(2)})\in\mathbf D_i^{(2)}\otimes 1+1\otimes \mathbf D_i^{(2)}+E_i^{(1)}\otimes F_i^{(1)}+\mathbb{C}^{\times} E_{i-1}^{(1)}\otimes F_{i-1}^{(1)}+\big(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{+}\big)^2\otimes \big(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{-}\big)^2.
\end{align*}
Note that $\Delta(E_i^{(1)})=E_i^{(1)}\otimes 1+1\otimes E_i^{(1)}$. Using $[\mathbf D_i^{(2)},E_i^{(r)}]=\mathfrak{s}_iE_i^{(r+1)}$, $[F_i^{(1)},E_i^{(s)}]=\mathfrak{s}_i H_i^{(s)}$, and $[E_i^{(r)},\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{-}]\subset \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\leqslant0}$, one shows inductively Part (2). Similarly, one proves Part (3).

We then prove Part (1). It is clearly for the case $i=1$. By \eqref{eq:def-H}, it suffices to prove the statement with $D$ replaced by $H$. Applying $[\Delta(F_i^{(1)}),?]$ to Part (2) and using $[F_i^{(1)},E_i^{(s)}]=\mathfrak{s}_i H_i^{(s)}$, we find that
\[
\Delta(H_i^{(r)})-\sum_{s=0}^r H_i^{(s)}\otimes H_i^{(r)}\in \Big[F_i^{(1)},\big(\mathrm{K}_{m|n}^{>0}\big)^2\Big]\otimes \mathrm{K}_{m|n}^{<0}.
\]
Similarly, applying $[\Delta(E_i^{(1)}),?]$ to Part (3), we have
\[
\Delta(H_i^{(r)})-\sum_{s=0}^r H_i^{(s)}\otimes H_i^{(r)}\in \mathrm{K}_{m|n}^{>0}\otimes \Big[E_i^{(1)},\big(\mathrm{K}_{m|n}^{<0}\big)^2\Big].
\]
Combining the two equations above completes the proof of Part (1).

title: Proof
body_md:
When $\sigma=0$ and $\mathfrak{s}$ is the standard one, it is well known \cite{Go07,Na20} that the set $\{\mathcal C_{m|n}^{(r)}\,|\,r\geqslant1\}$ is algebraically independent and it generates $\mathcal Z(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n})$. For a general $\mathfrak{s}$, the proof in the standard case works analogously as in \cite[Thm.~2.43]{Ts20}.

We claim that $\mathcal Z(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n})= \mathcal Z(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma))$ for any $\sigma$.
Note that $D_i^{(r)}$ belongs to $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^0 \subseteq \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$ for all $1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n, r>0$. Then \eqref{eq:Ber} implies that $\mathcal Z(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n})\subseteq\mathcal Z(\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma))$.
The other inclusion can be established by passing to the associated graded superalgebra ${\mathrm{gr}}^L\, \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)$ with respect to the loop filtration, with the help of \cite[Thm.~4.4]{Pe21} and \cite[Prop.~3.8]{Na20}, and modifying the argument in \cite[Thm. 1.7.5]{Mo07}.

label: thm:grownup
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:grownup}
Let $\sigma$ be a shift matrix and write $\sigma = \sigma^\prime + \sigma^{\prime\prime}$ 
where $\sigma^\prime$ is strictly lower triangular and
$\sigma^{\prime\prime}$ is strictly upper triangular. 
Identify $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma), \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^\prime)$ and $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})$ as subalgebras of $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$. Then the restriction of the comultiplication
$\Delta:\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{m|n} \otimes \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$ 
gives a homomorphism
\begin{equation*}
\Delta:\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^\prime) \otimes \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}).
\end{equation*}
Moreover, for $\ell^\prime \geqslant s_{m+n,1}, \ell^{\prime\prime} \geqslant s_{1,m+n}$ and $\ell = \ell^\prime + \ell^{\prime\prime}$,
this map $\Delta$ factors through the quotients to define a homomorphism
$\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^\ell(\sigma)
\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^\prime}(\sigma^\prime) \otimes \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^{\prime\prime}}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})$
which, after identifying
$\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell}(\sigma)\cong W(\pi)$, 
$\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^\prime}(\sigma^\prime) \cong W(\pi^\prime)$ and
$\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^{\prime\prime}}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})\cong W(\pi^{\prime\prime})$,
is precisely the parabolic induction $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}$ defined in \eqref{Wdel}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall from \cite[Rmk. 8.5]{Pe21} that $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma), \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^\prime)$, and $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})$ are identified with the inverse limits ${\displaystyle  \lim_{\leftarrow}\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^\ell(\sigma),  \lim_{\leftarrow}\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^\prime}(\sigma^\prime)}$, and ${\displaystyle\lim_{\leftarrow}\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}^{\ell^{\prime\prime}}(\sigma^{\prime\prime})}$, respectively. 
The commutative diagram in Corollary \ref{comWdel} ensures that the maps $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}$ are stable as $\ell^\prime, \ell^{\prime\prime}\rightarrow \infty$, showing the existence of the induced homomorphism 
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{\leftarrow}\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}:\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)\rightarrow \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^\prime)\otimes \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma^{\prime\prime}),
\end{equation*}
lifting from the maps $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}$ for all $\ell^\prime\geqslant s_{m+n,1}, \ell^{\prime\prime}\geqslant s_{1,m+n}$.
It remains to show that ${\displaystyle \lim_{\leftarrow}\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}}$ agrees with the restriction of $\Delta$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)$.

Let $X$ denote some generator $D_i^{(r)}, E_{i}^{(r)}$ or $F_{i}^{(r)}$ of $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)\subseteq \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$. Its image $\Delta(X)$ can be calculated as follows: first express $X$ in terms of a linear combination of monomials in $\mathsf{T}_{i,j}^{(r)}$ by the explicit formulas in \cite[Prop. 3.1]{Pe16}. 
Then by \eqref{coproduct}, $\Delta(X)$ equals a linear combination of monomials in $\mathsf{T}_{h,k}^{(s)}$.
Finally we rewrite all $\mathsf{T}_{h,k}^{(s)}$ appearing in the expression back in terms of the generators $D_i^{(r)}, E_{i}^{(r)}$ and $F_{i}^{(r)}$.
On the other hand, exactly the same procedure can be applied to calculate $\Delta_{\ell^\prime, \ell^{\prime\prime}}(X)$ where $X$ runs over generators $D_i^{(r)}, E_{i}^{(r)}$ or $F_{i}^{(r)}$ in $W(\pi)$ for each $\ell$, using \eqref{omega2} and \eqref{coproductW}.
The crucial point is that the formulas expressing $\mathsf{T}_{i,j;0}^{(r)}$ in terms of $D_i^{(r)}, E_{i}^{(r)}$ and $F_{i}^{(r)}$ in $\mathrm{U}(\mathfrak{p})$ is completely the same as the explicit formula in \cite[Prop. 3.1]{Pe16}, for both of them are deduced from applying Gauss decomposition to an invertible matrix.
This shows that ${\displaystyle \lim_{\leftarrow}\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}} =\Delta}$.

label: rem:row-shift
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:row-shift}
In fact, {\em all} parabolic inductions $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}:W(\pi)\rightarrow W(\pi^\prime)\otimes W(\pi^{\prime\prime})$ can be expressed in terms of the comultiplication $\Delta$ on $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$ as follows.
Let $\vec{\pi}^\prime$ denote the right-justified pyramid with the same row lengths as $\pi^\prime$, and let $\vec{\pi}^{\prime\prime}$ denote the left-justified pyramid with the same row lengths as $\pi^{\prime\prime}$. Let $\vec{\pi}=\vec{\pi}^\prime \otimes \vec{\pi}^{\prime\prime}$.
Note that the parabolic induction $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}:W(\pi)\rightarrow W(\pi^\prime)\otimes W(\pi^{\prime\prime})$ can be recovered from $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}:W(\vec\pi)\rightarrow W(\vec{\pi}^\prime)\otimes W(\vec{\pi}^{\prime\prime})$ by Lemma \ref{lem:paraiota}, using the isomorphisms $\iota$. Now $\Delta_{\ell^\prime,\ell^{\prime\prime}}:W(\vec\pi)\rightarrow W(\vec{\pi}^\prime)\otimes W(\vec{\pi}^{\prime\prime})$ is one of the comultiplications described by Theorem~\ref{thm:grownup}.

label: thmHC
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmHC}
Let $\mathfrak{s}$ be an arbitrary parity sequence of type $(M|N)$. We have the following.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The homomorphism $\operatorname{HC}:Z(\mathfrak{g})\rightarrow I(\mathfrak{c})$ is an algebra isomorphism. 
\item The map $\operatorname{HC}:Z(\mathfrak{g})\rightarrow S(\mathfrak{c})$ is independent of the choice of the parity sequence $\mathfrak{s}$ (equivalently, independent of the choice of the normal order $\lhd$).
\item We have 
\[\operatorname{HC}^\mathfrak{s}(z_{M|N,\mathfrak{s}}(u))=\prod_{i\in {\mathbb I}} (u+\omega_i)^{\mathfrak{s}_i}=\prod_{k=1}^{M}(u+x_k) \bigg/ \prod_{t=1}^N(u+y_t),\]
where the product in the middle expression is written from left to right increasingly with respect to the normal ordering on ${\mathbb I}$ determined by $\mathfrak{s}$, and $\omega_j=e_{j,j}=x_{j'}$ if $\mathfrak{s}_j=1$ and $\omega_j=-e_{j,j}=y_{j'}$  if $\mathfrak{s}_j=-1$ with $$j':=\#\left\{1\leqslant i < j \: \big| \: \mathfrak{s}_i = \mathfrak{s}_j \right\} +1.$$
\item In particular, the coefficients $\{z_{M|N,\mathfrak{s}}^{(r)}\,|\,r\geqslant 1\}$ of $z_{M|N,\mathfrak{s}}(u)$ generate the center $Z(\mathrm U(\mathfrak{gl}_{M|N}))$. 
Moreover, $\operatorname{HC}^\mathfrak{s}(z_{M|N,\mathfrak{s}}^{(r)})=e_r(x_1,\ldots,x_M/y_1,\ldots,y_N)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Part (1) is due to Kac and Sergeev, see \cite[\S13.2]{Mus12} for details. Part (2) is established in \cite[Thm.~2.2]{BG19} while Part (3) for the standard parity sequence is obtained in \cite[Thm.~2.3]{BG19}. Part (4) follows from Parts (1)-(3).

Part (3) for a general parity sequence $\mathfrak{s}$ follows from Part (2) and the statement for the standard parity case. Here we provide a more direct approach. By the explicit decomposition of the quantum Berezinian $\mathcal C_{M|N}(u)$ with respect to an arbitrary parity sequence given in \eqref{eq:Ber}, together with the fact that the evaluation map  $\operatorname{ev}:\mathrm Y_{M|N} \rightarrow \mathrm U(\mathfrak{gl}_{M|N})$ from \eqref{evahom} is a homomorphism, one deduces that
\[
z_{M|N,\mathfrak{s}}(u)= \prod_{i=1}^{M+N} (u-\kappa_i)^{\mathfrak{s}_i}\operatorname{ev}( \mathcal C_{M|N}(u)).
\] 
By \eqref{def:HC}, the Harish-Chandra map $\operatorname{HC}^\mathfrak{s}$ with respect to $\mathfrak{s}$ carries the correct translations to each $e_{j,j}$, deducing the desired expression.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the highest $\bm\ell$-weight vector $w_{\bm\zeta}$ in the Verma module $\mathcal M(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$. Then it follows from \eqref{dr5} and \eqref{eq:def-H} that
\[
E_{i}^{(r)}F_i^{(s)}w_{\bm\zeta}=[E_{i}^{(r)},F_i^{(s)}]w_{\bm\zeta}=
-\mathfrak{s}_{i+1}H_i^{(r+s-1)}w_{\bm\zeta}=0
\]
for all $1\leqslant i<m+n$, $r>s_{i,i+1}$, and $s>s_{i+1,i}$ due to our choice of $\bm\zeta$. Indeed, by \eqref{eq:def-H} we have  that $H_i(u)w_{\bm\zeta}=u^{-d_i}Q_i(u)w_{\bm\zeta}$ and hence $H_i^{(r+s-1)}w_{\bm\zeta}=0$ if $r>s_{i,i+1}$ and $s>s_{i+1,i}$. Thus the unique maximal proper submodule in $\mathcal M(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$ is generated by  all $F_i^{(s)}w_{\bm\zeta}$ for $1\leqslant i<m+n$ and $s>s_{i+1,i}$, completing the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
($\Rightarrow$). Let $\sigma_j$ denote the $2\times 2$ submatrix
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
s_{j,j} & s_{j,j+1}\\
s_{j+1,j} & s_{j+1,j+1}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
of the shift matrix $\sigma$. The map $\psi_j:\mathrm{Y}_{\mathfrak{s}_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j+1}}(\sigma_j)\to {\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$ defined by
\[
\psi_j:\mathrm{Y}_{\mathfrak{s}_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j+1}}(\sigma_j)\to {\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)},\quad D_k^{(r)}\mapsto D_{j+k-1}^{(r)},~E_1^{(r)}\mapsto E_j^{(r)},~F_1^{(r)}\mapsto F_j^{(r)},\quad k=1,2,
\]
induces an embedding of the shifted (super) Yangian $\mathrm{Y}_{\mathfrak{s}_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j+1}}(\sigma_j)$ into ${\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$. Then the highest $\bm\ell$-weight vector $v_{\bm\lambda}$ remains to be a highest $\bm\ell$-weight vector of highest $\bm\ell$-weight $\bm\lambda_j=(\lambda_j(u),\lambda_{j+1}(u))$ over the (super)algebra $\mathrm{Y}_{\mathfrak{s}_{j}\mathfrak{s}_{j+1}}(\sigma_j)$. Note that $\mathfrak{s}$ is the standard parity sequence. If $1\leqslant j<m+n$ and $j\ne m$, then $\mathfrak{s}_j=\mathfrak{s}_{j+1}$ and hence \eqref{eq:fd-criterion} with the corresponding restrictions follows from \cite[Coro.~7.5]{BK08}. If $j=m$, then $\mathfrak{s}_m\ne \mathfrak{s}_{m+1}$ and hence \eqref{eq:fd-criterion} follows from Proposition \ref{prop:rk1}.

($\Leftarrow$). Recalling the isomorphism $\iota$ from \eqref{iotadef}, the twist of a highest $\bm\ell$-weight $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\vec{\sigma})$-module by $\iota$ is again a highest $\bm\ell$-weight ${\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$-module with the same highest $\bm\ell$-weight. Moreover, the twist of a module in $\mathcal O_{\vec{\sigma}}$ is in $\mathcal O_\sigma$. Thus it suffices to prove it for the case when $\sigma$ is an upper shift matrix. Then we have the coproduct $\Delta:{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}\to \mathrm{Y}_{m|n}\otimes{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$. Rewrite $\bm\lambda$ as a product $\bm\lambda=\bm\gamma\bm\zeta$ such that
\[
\frac{\gamma_j(u)}{\gamma_{j+1}(u)}=\frac{P_j(u)}{P_j(u-\mathfrak{s}_j)}, \quad \frac{\gamma_m(u)}{\gamma_{m+1}(u)}=\frac{P_m(u)}{Q_m(u)},\quad \frac{\zeta_j(u)}{\zeta_{j+1}(u)}=\frac{u^{d_j}}{Q_j(u)},\quad \frac{\zeta_m(u)}{\zeta_{m+1}(u)}=1,
\]
for $1\leqslant j<m+n$ and $j\ne m$. Via the coproduct, we have the ${\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$-module $\mathcal L(\bm\gamma)\boxtimes \mathcal L(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$, where $\mathcal L(\bm\gamma)$ is the irreducible $\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}$-module with highest $\bm\ell$-weight $\bm\gamma$. Let $v_{\bm\gamma}$ and $v_{\bm \zeta}$ be the corresponding highest $\bm\ell$-weight vectors in $\mathcal L(\bm\gamma)$ and $\mathcal L(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$, respectively. It follows from Lemma \ref{lem:tensor} that $v_{\bm\gamma}\otimes v_{\bm \zeta}$ is a highest $\bm\ell$-weight vector of $\bm\ell$-weight $\bm\lambda$. Thus $\mathcal L(\sigma,\bm\lambda)$ is isomorphic to a sub-quotient of $\mathcal L(\bm\gamma)\boxtimes \mathcal L(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$. By \cite[Thm.~4]{Zh96}, $\mathcal L(\bm\gamma)$ is finite dimensional. Therefore, the statement follows as $\mathcal L(\sigma,\bm\zeta)$ is 1-dimensional by Lemma \ref{lem:1-dim}.

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to prove Part (2) as Part (1) follows by  a similar filtration argument in the proof of \cite[Thm.~5.5]{BK08}. Recall that the Verma module $\mathcal M(\sigma,\bm\lambda)$ is the quotient of ${\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}$ by the left ideal $\mathcal J$ generated by the elements
\[
\big\{D_i^{(r)}-\lambda_i^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n,r>0\big\}\cup\big\{E_{i}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i \leqslant m+n,r>s_{i,i+1}\big\}.
\]
It is not hard to see from \eqref{gedef} and the Gauss decomposition \eqref{eq:GD-shift} the left ideal $\mathcal J$ is also equivalently generated by the elements
\[
P:=\big\{T_{i,i}^{(r)}-\lambda_i^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n,r>0\big\}\cup\big\{T_{i,j}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m+n,r>s_{i,j}\big\}.
\]
Let $Q:=\big\{T_{j,i}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m+n,r>s_{j,i}\big\}$. Pick any ordering on $P\cup Q$ such that the elements of $Q$ precede the elements of $P$. Clearly, it follows from Lemma \ref{lem:PBW-T} and Proposition \ref{prop:PBW-Verma-Y} that the ordered supermonomials in the elements $P\cup Q$ containing at least one element from $P$ form a basis of $\mathcal J$.

The $W(\pi)$-module $W(\pi)\otimes_{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}\mathcal M(\sigma,\bm\lambda)$ can be identified as the quotient of $W(\pi)$ by the image $\bar{\mathcal J}$ of $\mathcal J$ under the quotient map $\Omega:{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}\to W(\pi)$. 

If $\lambda_i^{(r)}\ne 0$ for some $1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n$ and $r>p_i$ (which is exactly $u^{p_i}\lambda_i(u)\notin\mathbb{C}[u]$), then it follows from Theorem \ref{thm:vanish} that the image of $T_{i,i}^{(r)}-\lambda_i^{(r)}$ is a unit in $W(\pi)$ and hence $W(\pi)\otimes_{\mathrm{Y}_{m|n}(\sigma)}\mathcal M(\sigma,\bm\lambda)=0$.

Conversely, suppose $u^{p_i}\lambda_i(u)\in\mathbb{C}[u]$. Consider two sets
\begin{align*}
\overline P:=&\,\big\{T_{i,i}^{(r)}-\lambda_i^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n,\,0<r\leqslant p_i\big\}\\
&\,\cup\big\{T_{i,j}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m+n,\,s_{i,j}< r\leqslant s_{i,j}+p_i\big\} 
\end{align*}
and $\overline Q:=\big\{T_{j,i}^{(r)}\mid 1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m+n,\,s_{j,i}<r\leqslant s_{j,i}+p_i\big\}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:vanish} and Lemma \ref{prop:PBW-T-truncated}, the order supermonomials in elements of $\overline P\cup \overline Q$ containing at least one element from $\overline P$ form a basis of $\bar{\mathcal J}$. Therefore, the image of $\mathcal Y$ forms a basis for $W(\pi)/\bar{\mathcal J}$, completing the proof of Part (2).

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Part (2) follows from Part (1) and Corollary \ref{cor:char}. Thus it suffices to prove Part (1).

Suppose $\mathcal M(\mathbf{A})$ is reducible, then we can assume $\mathcal L(\mathbf{B})$ is a subquotient of $\mathcal M(\mathbf{A})$, where $\mathbf{B}\in\mathrm{Row}(\pi)$ with entries $b_{i,1},\dots,b_{i,p_i}$ on its $i$-th row for each $1\leqslant i\leqslant m+n$ and $\mathbf{A}\ne \mathbf{B}$. Therefore the  $\bm\ell$-weight corresponding to the highest $\bm\ell$-weight vector of $\mathcal L(\mathbf{B})$ is $\prod_{i=1}^{m+n}\prod_{j=1}^{p_i}y_{i,b_{i,j}}$. Hence there exists a supertuple $c=(c_{i,j,k})_{1\leqslant i<k\leqslant m+n,1\leqslant j\leqslant p_i}$ such that
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{m+n}\prod_{j=1}^{p_i}y_{i,b_{i,j}}=\prod_{i=1}^{m+n}\prod_{j=1}^{p_i}\left(y_{i,a_{i,j}-\mathfrak{s}_i(c_{i,j,i+1}+\dots+c_{i,j,m+n})}\prod_{k=i+1}^{m+n}\Big(\frac{y_{k,a_{i,j}-\mathfrak{s}_i(c_{i,j,k+1}+\dots+c_{i,j,m+n})}}{y_{k,a_{i,j}-\mathfrak{s}_i(c_{i,j,k}+\dots+c_{i,j,m+n})}}\Big)^{\mathfrak{s}_i\mathfrak{s}_k}\right).
\]
Since $\mathbf{A}\ne \mathbf{B}$, the supertuple $c$ is non-trivial. Let ${\mathfrak i}$ be maximal such that $c_{i,j,{\mathfrak i}}\ne 0$ for some $1\leqslant i<{\mathfrak i}$ and $1\leqslant j\leqslant p_i$. Then we have
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{p_{\mathfrak i}}y_{{\mathfrak i},b_{{\mathfrak i},j}}=\prod_{j=1}^{p_{\mathfrak i}} y_{{\mathfrak i},a_{{\mathfrak i},j}}\prod_{i=1}^{{\mathfrak i}-1}\prod_{j=1}^{p_i}\Big(\frac{y_{{\mathfrak i},a_{i,j}}}{y_{{\mathfrak i},a_{i,j}-\mathfrak{s}_{\mathfrak i}c_{i,j,{\mathfrak i}}}}\Big)^{\mathfrak{s}_i\mathfrak{s}_{\mathfrak i}}.
\]
Since $a_{i_1,j_1}-a_{i_2,j_2}\notin \mathbb{Z}$ for $(i_1,j_1)\ne (i_2,j_2)$, there is no way to rewrite the RHS as a monomial in $y_{{\mathfrak i},b_{{\mathfrak i},j}}$ as the LHS. Hence we obtain a contradiction, completing the proof.

body_md: We need to show that $[\mu(z),h]=0$ for $z\in Z(W(\pi))$ and $h\in \mathrm{U}(\mathfrak{h})$. By the standard fact that the annihilator of any Zariski dense set of Verma (super)modules is zero (see e.g. \cite[Proof of Lem.~13.1.4]{Mus12}), it suffices to check that $[\mu(z),h]$ annihilates $\mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_1)\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes\mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_\ell)$ for generic $\mathbf{A}\in \mathrm{Tab}(\pi)$ with columns $\mathbf{A}_1,\dots,\mathbf{A}_{\ell}$. title: Proof
body_md:
The injectivity of $\psi$ follows from that of $\operatorname{HC}$ and the commutative diagram \eqref{HChc}.
It remains to prove that $\psi$ is surjective. Since $\operatorname{hc}\circ\mu$ is injective and we know $\operatorname{HC}\big( Z(\mathrm{U}(\mathfrak{g})) \big)=I(\mathfrak{c})$ by Theorem \ref{thmHC}, it suffices to show $\operatorname{hc}\circ \mu\big(Z(W(\pi))\big)\subseteq I(\mathfrak{c})$.  Note that the image of $\operatorname{hc}$ is contained in $I(\mathfrak{c}_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes I(\mathfrak{c}_\ell)$. It reduces to show that $\operatorname{hc}\circ\mu\big(Z(W(\pi))\big)\subset S(\mathfrak c)^{\mathfrak{S}_M\times \mathfrak{S}_N}$ as $I(\mathfrak{c})=\big(I(\mathfrak{c}_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes I(\mathfrak{c}_\ell)\big)\cap \big(S(\mathfrak c)^{\mathfrak{S}_M\times \mathfrak{S}_N}\big)$. 

Let $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ be $\pi$-tableaux that share the same content in even and odd boxes, respectively. By the definition of the Harish-Chandra homomorphism, to show $\operatorname{hc}\circ\mu\big(Z(W(\pi))\big)\subset S(\mathfrak c)^{\mathfrak{S}_M\times \mathfrak{S}_N}$, we need to show that any element $z\in Z( W(\pi) )$ acts on the modules $\mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_1)\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes\mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_\ell)$ and $\mathcal M(\mathbf{B}_1)\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes\mathcal M(\mathbf{B}_\ell)$ by the same scalar, where $\mathbf{A}_i$ and $\mathbf{B}_i$ denote the $i$-th column of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, respectively.
Similar to the argument in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:mucent1}, it suffices to prove the statement for generic $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, since the set of generic $\pi$-tableaux is Zariski dense in the set of all $\pi$-tableaux.

If $\mathbf{B}$ is obtained from $\mathbf{A}$ by permuting even (resp. odd) entries within columns, then this is obvious since the image of $\operatorname{hc}$ is contained in $I(\mathfrak{c}_1) \otimes \cdots \otimes I(\mathfrak{c}_\ell)$.

If $\mathbf{B}$ is obtained from $\mathbf{A}$ by permuting even (resp. odd) entries within rows, then by \eqref{eq:Verma-W}--\eqref{eq:lam-tab} we have $\mathcal M(\mathbf{A})=\mathcal M(\mathbf{B})$. Since $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are generic, then by Lemma \ref{lem:simple-generic} we have 
\[
\mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_1)\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes \mathcal M(\mathbf{A}_\ell)\cong \mathcal M(\mathbf{A})=\mathcal M(\mathbf{B})\cong \mathcal M(\mathbf{B}_1)\boxtimes\cdots \boxtimes \mathcal M(\mathbf{B}_\ell),
\] 
as irreducible $W(\pi)$-modules. As a consequence, any element $z\in Z( W(\pi) )$ acts on these modules by exactly the same scalar. The general case follows from these two special cases.
